Guidance for AI coding agents working with this repository.

Fizzy is a kanban-style project management and issue tracker: cards move across columns on boards, with comments, mentions, and assignments.

## Deploy

Default branch: `main`

Self-hosted deploys run Kamal against `config/deploy.yml` — see `docs/kamal-deployment.md`.

## SaaS mode

For local agent work, `tmp/saas.txt` is the checkout-level SaaS switch used by `bin/setup`. When present, read `saas/AGENTS.md` before continuing. Otherwise, do not apply its instructions.

## Architecture Overview

### Multi-Tenancy (URL-Based)

Fizzy uses **URL path-based multi-tenancy**:
- Accounts have a unique decimal `external_account_id` used in URL prefixes
- URLs are prefixed: `/{account_id}/boards/...`
- Middleware (`AccountSlug::Extractor`) extracts the account ID from the URL and sets `Current.account`
- The slug is moved from `PATH_INFO` to `SCRIPT_NAME`, making Rails think it's "mounted" at that path
- Tenant-scoped domain records are account-isolated; global identity, session, and authentication records are exceptions
- Background jobs automatically serialize and restore account context

**Key insight**: This architecture allows multi-tenancy without subdomains or separate databases, making local development and testing simpler.

### Authentication & Authorization

Passwordless magic link authentication. A global `Identity` (email-based) can have `Users` in multiple Accounts, so an email is not a single account membership. Users have roles: owner, admin, member, system. Board-level access control via `Access` records.

### Entropy System

Cards automatically "postpone" (move to "not now") after inactivity:
- Account-level default entropy period
- Board-level entropy override
- Prevents endless todo lists from accumulating
- Configurable via Account/Board settings

### UUID Primary Keys

All tables use UUIDs (UUIDv7 format, base36-encoded as 25-char strings):
- Custom fixture UUID generation maintains deterministic ordering for tests
- Fixtures are always "older" than runtime records
- `.first`/`.last` work correctly in tests

### Background Jobs (Solid Queue)

Database-backed job queue (no Redis):
- Custom `FizzyActiveJobExtensions` prepended to ActiveJob
- Jobs automatically capture/restore `Current.account`
- Mission Control::Jobs for monitoring

Recurring tasks are declared in `config/recurring.yml`.

### Sharded Full-Text Search

Full-text search runs in the database, not Elasticsearch. On MySQL it is sharded 16 ways by CRC32 of the account ID (`Search::Record::Trilogy`); on SQLite it is a single FTS5 index (`Search::Record::SQLite`). Don't assume the sharded shape when working under SQLite. Models in `app/models/search/`.

### Imports and exports

Allow people to move between OSS and SAAS Fizzy instances:
- Exports/Imports can be written to/read from local or S3 storage depending on the config of the instance (both must be supported)
- Must be able to handle very large ZIP files (500+GB)
- Models in `app/models/account/data_transfer/`, `app/models/zip_file`

## Invocation order

We order methods vertically based on their invocation order. This helps us to understand the flow of the code.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    method_1
    method_2
  end

  private
    def method_1

Should I call a method `do_something` or `do_something!`?

As a general rule, we only use `!` for methods that have a correspondent counterpart without `!`. In particular, we don’t use `!` to flag destructive actions. There are plenty of destructive methods in Ruby and Rails that do not end with `!`.

end
```

If a module only has private methods, we mark it `private` at the top and add an extra new line after but don't indent.

```ruby
module SomeModule
  private
  
  def some_private_method
    # ...
  end
end
```

## CRUD controllers

We model web endpoints as CRUD operations on resources (REST). When an action doesn't map cleanly to a standard CRUD verb, we introduce a new resource rather than adding custom actions.

```ruby
# Bad
resources :cards do
  post :close
  post :reopen
end

# Good
resources :cards do
  resource :closure
end
```

## Controller and model interactions

In general, we favor a [vanilla Rails](https://dev.37signals.com/vanilla-rails-is-plenty/) approach with thin controllers directly invoking a rich domain model. We don't use services or other artifacts to connect the two.

Invoking plain Active Record operations is totally fine:

```ruby
class Cards::CommentsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @comment = @card.comments.create!(comment_params)
  end
end
```

For more complex behavior, we prefer clear, intention-revealing model APIs that controllers call directly:

```ruby
class Cards::GoldnessesController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @card.gild
  end
end
```

When justified, it is fine to use services or form objects, but don't treat those as special artifacts:

```ruby
Signup.new(email_address: email_address).create_identity
```

## Run async operations in jobs

As a general rule, we write shallow job classes that delegate the logic itself to domain models:

* We typically use the suffix `_later` to flag methods that enqueue a job.
* A common scenario is having a model class that enqueues a job that, when executed, invokes some method in that same class. In this case, we use the suffix `_now` for the regular synchronous method.

```ruby
module Event::Relaying
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit :relay_later
  end

  def relay_later
    Event::RelayJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def relay_now
    # ...
  end
end

class Card < ApplicationRecord
  include Accessible, Assignable, Attachments, Broadcastable, Closeable, Colored, Commentable,
    Entropic, Eventable, Exportable, Golden, Mentions, Multistep, Pinnable, Postponable, Promptable,
    Readable, Searchable, Stallable, Statuses, Storage::Tracked, Taggable, Triageable, Watchable

  belongs_to :account, default: -> { board.account }
  belongs_to :board
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  has_many :reactions, -> { order(:created_at) }, as: :reactable, dependent: :delete_all
  has_one_attached :image, dependent: :purge_later

  has_rich_text :description

  before_save :set_default_title, if: :published?
  before_create :assign_number

  after_save   -> { board.touch }, if: :published?
  after_touch  -> { board.touch }, if: :published?
  after_update :handle_board_change, if: :saved_change_to_board_id?

  scope :reverse_chronologically, -> { order created_at:     :desc, id: :desc }
  scope :chronologically,         -> { order created_at:     :asc,  id: :asc  }
  scope :latest,                  -> { order last_active_at: :desc, id: :desc }
  scope :with_users,              -> { preload(creator: [ :avatar_attachment, :account ], assignees: [ :avatar_attachment, :account ]) }
  scope :preloaded,               -> { with_users.preload(:column, :tags, :steps, :closure, :goldness, :activity_spike, :image_attachment, reactions: :reacter, board: [ :entropy, :columns ], not_now: [ :user ]).with_rich_text_description_and_embeds }

  scope :indexed_by, ->(index) do
    case index
    when "stalled" then stalled
    when "postponing_soon" then postponing_soon
    when "closed" then closed
    when "maybe" then awaiting_triage
    when "not_now" then postponed.latest
    when "golden" then golden
    when "draft" then drafted
    else all
    end
  end

  scope :sorted_by, ->(sort) do
    case sort
    when "newest" then reverse_chronologically
    when "oldest" then chronologically
    when "latest" then latest
    else latest
    end
  end

  def card
    self
  end

  def to_param
    number.to_s
  end

  def move_to(new_board)
    transaction do
      card.update!(board: new_board)
      card.events.update_all(board_id: new_board.id)
      Event.where(eventable: card.comments).update_all(board_id: new_board.id)
    end
  end

  def filled?
    title.present? || description.present?
  end

  private
    def set_default_title
      self.title = "Untitled" if title.blank?
    end

    def handle_board_change
      old_board = account.boards.find_by(id: board_id_before_last_save)

      transaction do
        update! column: nil
        track_board_change_event(old_board.name)
        grant_access_to_assignees unless board.all_access?
      end

      remove_inaccessible_notifications_later
      clean_inaccessible_data_later
    end

    def track_board_change_event(old_board_name)
      track_event "board_changed", particulars: { old_board: old_board_name, new_board: board.name }
    end

    def assign_number
      self.number ||= account.with_lock { account.increment!(:cards_count).cards_count }
    end

# Adds database-agnostic date arithmetic methods to ActiveRecord adapters.
# This allows code to perform date calculations without checking which database adapter is in use.
#
# Usage:
#   connection.date_subtract("created_at", "3600")
#   # MySQL/Trilogy: "DATE_SUB(created_at, INTERVAL 3600 SECOND)"
#   # SQLite: "datetime(created_at, '-' || (3600) || ' seconds')"

# Module for MySQL-based adapters (Trilogy, Mysql2, etc.)
module MysqlDateArithmetic
  # Generates SQL for subtracting seconds from a date/time column in MySQL.
  #
  # @param date_column [String] The date/time column or expression
  # @param seconds_expression [String] SQL expression that evaluates to number of seconds
  # @return [String] MySQL DATE_SUB expression
  #
  # Example:
  #   date_subtract("last_active_at", "COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600)")
  #   # => "DATE_SUB(last_active_at, INTERVAL COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600) SECOND)"
  def date_subtract(date_column, seconds_expression)
    "DATE_SUB(#{date_column}, INTERVAL #{seconds_expression} SECOND)"
  end
end

# Module for SQLite adapter
module SqliteDateArithmetic
  # Generates SQL for subtracting seconds from a date/time column in SQLite.
  #
  # @param date_column [String] The date/time column or expression
  # @param seconds_expression [String] SQL expression that evaluates to number of seconds
  # @return [String] SQLite datetime expression
  #
  # Example:
  #   date_subtract("last_active_at", "COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600)")
  #   # => "datetime(last_active_at, '-' || (COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600)) || ' seconds')"
  def date_subtract(date_column, seconds_expression)
    "datetime(#{date_column}, '-' || (#{seconds_expression}) || ' seconds')"
  end
end

ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_record) do
  # Prepend MySQL date arithmetic to AbstractMysqlAdapter (covers Trilogy, Mysql2, etc.)
  if defined?(ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::AbstractMysqlAdapter)
    ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::AbstractMysqlAdapter.prepend(MysqlDateArithmetic)
  end

  # Prepend SQLite date arithmetic to SQLite3Adapter
  if defined?(ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SQLite3Adapter)
    ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SQLite3Adapter.prepend(SqliteDateArithmetic)
  end
end

module Card::Closeable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_one :closure, dependent: :destroy

    scope :closed, -> { joins(:closure) }
    scope :open, -> { where.missing(:closure) }

    scope :recently_closed_first, -> { closed.order(closures: { created_at: :desc }) }
    scope :closed_at_window, ->(window) { closed.where(closures: { created_at: window }) }
    scope :closed_by, ->(users) { closed.where(closures: { user_id: Array(users) }) }
  end

  def closed?
    closure.present?
  end

  def open?
    !closed?
  end

  def closed_by
    closure&.user
  end

  def closed_at
    closure&.created_at
  end

  def close(user: Current.user)
    unless closed?
      transaction do
        not_now&.destroy
        create_closure! user: user
        track_event :closed, creator: user
      end
    end
  end

  def reopen(user: Current.user)
    if closed?
      transaction do
        closure&.destroy
        track_event :reopened, creator: user
      end
    end
  end
end

module Card::Postponable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_one :not_now, dependent: :destroy, class_name: "Card::NotNow"

    scope :active, -> { open.published.where.missing(:not_now) }
  end

  def postponed?

  def postponed_at

  end

  def active?

  end

  def auto_postpone(**args)

  end

  def postpone(user: Current.user, event_name: :postponed)
    transaction do
      send_back_to_triage(skip_event: true)
      reopen
      activity_spike&.destroy
      create_not_now!(user: user) unless postponed?
      track_event event_name, creator: user
    end
  end

  def resume
    transaction do
      reopen
      activity_spike&.destroy
      not_now&.destroy
    end
  end
end

require "test_helper"

class Card::EntropicTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  setup do
    Current.session = sessions(:david)
  end

  test "auto_postpone_at uses the period defined in the account by default" do
    freeze_time

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    entropies("37s_account").reload.update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days
    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (365 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

  test "auto_postpone_at infers the period from the board when present" do
    freeze_time

    entropies(:writebook_board).update! auto_postpone_period: 90.days
    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (90 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

  test "setting auto_postpone_period in the board without entropy will create it, without affecting the account entropy" do
    account_entropy = entropies("37s_account")
    original_period = account_entropy.auto_postpone_period

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    boards(:writebook).update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days

    assert_equal original_period, account_entropy.reload.auto_postpone_period
  end

  test "auto postpone all due using the default account entropy" do
    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.ago - entropies("37s_account").auto_postpone_period)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.from_now - entropies("37s_account").auto_postpone_period)

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert_equal accounts("37s").system_user, cards(:logo).postponed_by
    assert_not cards(:shipping).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "auto postpone all due using entropy defined at the board level" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.ago - entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.from_now - entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period)

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert_not cards(:shipping).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "postponing soon scope" do
    cards(:logo, :shipping).each(&:published!)

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)

    assert_includes Card.postponing_soon, cards(:logo)
    assert_not_includes Card.postponing_soon, cards(:shipping)
  end

  test "auto postpone all due works properly cross-account" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)

# Automatically use UUID type for all binary(16) columns and generate defaults

module UuidPrimaryKeyDefault
  def load_schema!
    define_uuid_primary_key_pending_default
    super
  end

  private
    def define_uuid_primary_key_pending_default
      if uuid_primary_key?
        pending_attribute_modifications << PendingUuidDefault.new(primary_key)
      end
    rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid
      # Table doesn't exist yet
    end

    def uuid_primary_key?
      table_name && primary_key && schema_cache.columns_hash(table_name)[primary_key]&.type == :uuid
    end

    PendingUuidDefault = Struct.new(:name) do
      def apply_to(attribute_set)
        attribute_set[name] = attribute_set[name].with_user_default(-> { ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.generate })
      end
    end
end

module MysqlUuidAdapter
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  # Override lookup_cast_type to recognize binary(16) as UUID type
  def lookup_cast_type(sql_type)
    if sql_type == "binary(16)"
      ActiveRecord::Type.lookup(:uuid, adapter: :trilogy)
    else
      super
    end
  end

  # Override fetch_type_metadata to preserve UUID type and limit
  def fetch_type_metadata(sql_type, extra = "")

        type: :uuid,

# Fix for SQLite FTS5 virtual table schema dumping
# Rails has a bug where it doesn't handle FTS5 content= and content_rowid= options

module SQLiteFTS5SchemaDumperFix
  # Override the virtual_tables method to handle FTS5 syntax properly
  def virtual_tables(stream)
    # Query sqlite_master for all virtual tables
    virtual_table_sqls = @connection.select_rows(
      "SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND sql LIKE 'CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE%'"
    )

    virtual_table_sqls.each do |table_name, sql|
      # Just output the raw SQL since create_virtual_table doesn't handle our syntax
      stream.puts "  execute #{sql.inspect}"
      stream.puts
    end
  end
end

module ActiveRecord
  module Type
    class Uuid < Binary
      BASE36_LENGTH = 25 # 36^25 > 2^128

      class << self
        def generate
          uuid = SecureRandom.uuid_v7
          hex = uuid.delete("-")
          hex_to_base36(hex)
        end

        def hex_to_base36(hex)
          hex.to_i(16).to_s(36).rjust(BASE36_LENGTH, "0")
        end

        def base36_to_hex(base36)
          base36.to_s.to_i(36).to_s(16).rjust(32, "0")
        end
      end

      def serialize(value)
        return unless value

        binary = Uuid.base36_to_hex(value).scan(/../).map(&:hex).pack("C*")
        super(binary)
      end

      def deserialize(value)
        return unless value

        hex = value.to_s.unpack1("H*")
        Uuid.hex_to_base36(hex)
      end

      def cast(value)
        value
      end
    end
  end

module AccountSlug
  PATTERN = /(\d+)/
  PATH_INFO_MATCH = /\A(\/#{AccountSlug::PATTERN})/

  class Extractor
    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    # We're using account id prefixes in the URL path. Rather than namespace
    # all our routes, we're "mounting" the Rails app at this URL prefix.
    def call(env)
      request = ActionDispatch::Request.new(env)

      # $1, $2, $' == script_name, slug, path_info
      if request.script_name && request.script_name =~ PATH_INFO_MATCH
        # Likely due to restarting the action cable connection after upgrade
        env["fizzy.external_account_id"] = AccountSlug.decode($2)
      elsif request.path_info =~ PATH_INFO_MATCH
        # Yanks the prefix off PATH_INFO and move it to SCRIPT_NAME
        request.engine_script_name = request.script_name = $1
        request.path_info   = $'.empty? ? "/" : $'

        # Stash the account's Queenbee ID.
        env["fizzy.external_account_id"] = AccountSlug.decode($2)
      end

      if env["fizzy.external_account_id"]
        account = Account.find_by(external_account_id: env["fizzy.external_account_id"])
        Current.with_account(account) do
          @app.call env
        end
      else
        Current.without_account do
          @app.call env
        end
      end
    end
  end

  def self.decode(slug) slug.to_i end
  def self.encode(id) id.to_s end
end

Rails.application.config.middleware.insert_after Rack::TempfileReaper, AccountSlug::Extractor

**My Immediate Reaction: Testing, Testing, Testing!**

Okay, hold on a second! This theoretical discussion is interesting, but we're going too fast. I need to *see* this. Let's not just talk about it, let's actually *do* it. I'm going to build a 100,000-card SQLite database, and run the query directly against it. That's the only way to get a real handle on the performance. And, we *absolutely* need to include `ANALYZE` in the testing. Let's see how much that helps... or hinders.

Now, before we jump in, let's ground ourselves in a realistic scenario. What does a 100,000-card Fizzy install actually look like? It's not just a flat file. Typically, we're talking about a small number of accounts, maybe one, or a handful. We'll likely see a reasonable number of boards, let's say 10 to 50. And then the 100,000 cards. But it’s not all active at once. Realistically, we're going to have a *lot* of cards that are closed or postponed. I would imagine a distribution like this: 50,000 closed, 40,000 postponed, maybe 9,990 not due and 10 due – or possibly even zero due!

Okay, with that realistic model in mind, let's create a few test configurations: No `ANALYZE`, `ANALYZE` enabled (and then what does that actually *do* under the hood? Does it run `PRAGMA optimize` or not? And what are the Rails 8 implications?). And, to be thorough, let's also experiment with different table shapes.

Wait, hold up! Before we go further, I have a burning question! What is `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` *actually* doing when `sqlite_stat1` exists versus doesn't exist, and when there are 100,000 rows? I need to test that right now in a temporary SQLite file. Understanding the query plan is *critical* to understanding what's going on!

RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner '
require "benchmark"
require "sqlite3"
require "securerandom"

db_path = "/tmp/repro_entropy.sqlite3"
File.delete(db_path) if File.exist?(db_path)

# Copy schema from test sqlite db
src = SQLite3::Database.new("storage/test.sqlite3")
dst = SQLite3::Database.new(db_path)

src.execute("SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE sql IS NOT NULL AND type IN (\"table\", \"index\") AND name NOT LIKE \"sqlite_%\" AND name NOT LIKE \"search_records_fts%\"").each do |(sql)|
  dst.execute(sql)
end
src.close

dst.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = OFF")
dst.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")

now = Time.now.utc
def fmt(t)
  t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")
end

def uuid_blob(i)
  [0, 0, i].pack("Q>L>L>")
end

dst.transaction do
  # 1 account
  acc_id = uuid_blob(1)
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO accounts (id, name, cards_count, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [acc_id, "Test", 100000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO entropies (id, account_id, container_type, container_id, auto_postpone_period, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [uuid_blob(10), acc_id, "Account", acc_id, 2592000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])

  # 50 boards
  50.times do |b|
    bid = uuid_blob(100 + b)
    dst.execute("INSERT INTO boards (id, account_id, creator_id, name, all_access, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [bid, acc_id, uuid_blob(2), "Board #{b}", 1, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
    if b % 2 == 0
      dst.execute("INSERT INTO entropies (id, account_id, container_type, container_id, auto_postpone_period, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [uuid_blob(1000 + b), acc_id, "Board", bid, 2592000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
    end
  end

  # 100,000 cards: 50k closed, 40k not_now, 10k active (recent)
  card_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO cards (id, account_id, board_id, creator_id, number, status, title, last_active_at, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
  closure_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO closures (id, account_id, card_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
  not_now_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO card_not_nows (id, account_id, card_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")

  recent = fmt(now - 3600)
  old = fmt(now - 86400 * 60)

  100_000.times do |i|
    cid = uuid_blob(100_000 + i)
    bid = uuid_blob(100 + (i % 50))
    ts = (i < 90_000) ? old : recent
    card_stmt.execute(cid, acc_id, bid, uuid_blob(2), i + 1, "published", "Card #{i}", ts, ts, ts)
    if i < 50_000
      closure_stmt.execute(uuid_blob(500_000 + i), acc_id, cid, ts, ts)
    elsif i < 90_000
      not_now_stmt.execute(uuid_blob(600_000 + i), acc_id, cid, ts, ts)
    end
  end
  card_stmt.close
  closure_stmt.close
  not_now_stmt.close
end

sql = <<~SQL
  SELECT "cards".* FROM "cards"
  INNER JOIN "boards" ON "boards"."id" = "cards"."board_id"
  INNER JOIN "accounts" ON "accounts"."id" = "boards"."account_id"
  LEFT OUTER JOIN "entropies" ON "entropies"."container_type" = ? AND "entropies"."container_id" = "boards"."id"
  LEFT OUTER JOIN "closures" ON "closures"."card_id" = "cards"."id"
  LEFT OUTER JOIN "card_not_nows" AS "not_now" ON "not_now"."card_id" = "cards"."id"
  LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = \x27Account\x27 AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id
  WHERE "closures"."id" IS NULL AND "cards"."status" = ? AND "not_now"."id" IS NULL
    AND (last_active_at <= datetime(?, \x27-\x27 || (COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)) || \x27 seconds\x27))
  ORDER BY "cards"."id" ASC LIMIT ?
SQL

puts "=== BEFORE ANALYZE ==="
dst.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{sql}", ["Board", "published", fmt(now), 1000]).each { |r| puts r.join(" | ") }
t = Benchmark.realtime { @rows = dst.execute(sql, ["Board", "published", fmt(now), 1000]) }
puts "Rows: #{@rows.size}, Time: #{(t * 1000).round(2)}ms"

dst.execute("ANALYZE")
puts "\n=== AFTER ANALYZE ==="
dst.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{sql}", ["Board", "published", fmt(now), 1000]).each { |r| puts r.join(" | ") }
t = Benchmark.realtime { @rows = dst.execute(sql, ["Board", "published", fmt(now), 1000]) }
puts "Rows: #{@rows.size}, Time: #{(t * 1000).round(2)}ms"

dst.close
File.delete(db_path)
'

steps.reasoning_content:
**The Investigation Begins**

Whoa, hold on a minute! That initial script ran in 115 milliseconds, but production took a staggering 58 minutes and 9 seconds. Why such a massive difference?! I need to think like a detective and methodically identify EVERY difference between our test script and the production environment. Let's break it down:

1.  **Scale:** In the script, we had one account and 50 boards. What if the number of accounts and boards in the real system is very high?

2.  **The `find_each` Query:** The APM trace shows the `SolidQueue::RecurringJob#perform` job running for the massive time period with the SQL query taking up 99.9% of that time. The average execution time of the query over the last 30 days was 9m 41s, but now it's grown to nearly an hour! How can that be?! Is it executing this query once, taking a long time, or repeatedly in batches?

    *   **Possibility A:** Could a single, catastrophic query plan in SQLite be the culprit? It seems unlikely because the time is so high.
    *   **Possibility B:** Maybe the query is executed many times, perhaps 100 times? This would mean 100,000 cards are postponed and the amount of time taken by the individual queries would not add up to nearly an hour.

    Since the APM trace says 99.9% is `SELECT "cards".* FROM "cards" INNER JOIN "boards" ON ...`, it's almost certainly that **a single query took 58m 09s** to execute.

3.  **The Database Schema and Data Types:** Now the crucial question: Why would that SQL query take 58 minutes? It's time to dig into SQLite's query planner and the exact database schema, especially the data types used for our key columns. Did we use blobs in our script but text in reality?!

    *   I need to compare `db/schema_sqlite.rb` with the migration files, especially the initial schema file. Did any migration accidentally introduce a different column type or index than expected?
    *   Let's check the SQL of `Card.due_to_be_postponed` carefully, focusing on the join order! The order of the joins and the state of `sqlite_stat1` are very important, as is the bloom filter state.
    *   Could the outer table be the wrong table? Could the indices be wrong on `cards.board_id`, or `boards`, or `accounts`, or `entropies`? Could the `account_entropies` table be problematic?
    *   Could the version of SQLite or ActiveRecord's `find_each` have a negative impact?! What about BLOB vs TEXT affinity?

    *   Let's look at `closures`, `card_not_nows`, and `entropies`—do they have an `ANALYZE` or have different cardinalities, or no analyze?!
    *   What about the `sqlite_autoindex_cards_1` index, or the `ORDER BY`?

    *   What about the migrations themselves?

So, let's execute a systematic check:

1.  Examine all migrations, especially those related to `cards`, `boards`, `accounts`, `entropies`, `closures`, and `card_not_nows`.
2.  Determine exactly what `ActiveRecord::Base.connection` sends for `Card.due_to_be_postponed.find_each`, including the types of the bound parameters.
3.  Use `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on both system SQLite 3.46.1 and the gem-based SQLite 3.53.2 to see if there's a difference in their plans.
4.  Get `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for all combinations of row counts and index states.

#
# For string columns: defaults to 255 (MySQL's VARCHAR default)
#
# For text columns: converts MySQL's `size:` option to equivalent limits:
#   - (blank/default): 65,535 (TEXT)
#   - size: :tiny: 255 (TINYTEXT)
#   - size: :medium: 16,777,215 (MEDIUMTEXT)
#   - size: :long: 4,294,967,295 (LONGTEXT)
#

module TableDefinitionColumnLimits
  TEXT_SIZE_TO_LIMIT = {
    tiny: 255,
    medium: 16_777_215,
    long: 4_294_967_295
  }.freeze

  TEXT_DEFAULT_LIMIT = 65_535
  STRING_DEFAULT_LIMIT = 255

  def column(name, type, **options)
    if type == :string
      options[:limit] ||= STRING_DEFAULT_LIMIT
    end

    if type == :text || type == :binary
      if options.key?(:size)
        size = options.delete(:size)
        options[:limit] ||= TEXT_SIZE_TO_LIMIT.fetch(size) do
          raise ArgumentError, "Unknown text size: #{size.inspect}. Use :tiny, :medium, or :long"
        end
      elsif type == :text
        options[:limit] ||= TEXT_DEFAULT_LIMIT
      end
    end

    super
  end
end

# For SQLite: append inline CHECK constraints to enforce string/text length limits.
# since SQLite doesn't natively enforce VARCHAR/TEXT length limits.
module SQLiteColumnLimitCheckConstraints
  def add_column_options!(sql, options)
    super

    column = options[:column]
    if column && column.limit && %i[string text].include?(column.type)
      check_expr = if column.type == :string
        # VARCHAR limits are in characters
        %(length("#{column.name}") <= #{column.limit})
      else
        # TEXT limits are in bytes
        %(length(CAST("#{column.name}" AS BLOB)) <= #{column.limit})
      end
      sql << " CHECK(#{check_expr})"
    end

    sql
  end
end

steps.reasoning_content:
**Okay, let's break this down systematically. I need to be absolutely certain I understand every facet of this performance discrepancy.**

First, the immediate observation is that `db:migrate` produces identical tables and indexes to our schema file. However, my initial benchmarking script used a potentially flawed `last_active_at <= datetime(...)` condition, and I need to validate how Active Record handles `Card.due_to_be_postponed` with 100,000 cards in a *real* Active Record environment. This means a comprehensive examination of all related methods: `Card.auto_postpone_all_due`, `Card.due_to_be_postponed`, and `Card.postponing_soon`, along with realistic data shapes.

Diving deeper, I've noticed the code in `app/models/card/entropic.rb` constructs a complex `due_to_be_postponed` scope with multiple `JOIN` operations. The critical element is the `last_active_at` comparison using `connection.date_subtract` and `COALESCE` with `entropies` and `account_entropies`. I need to rigorously analyze the generated SQL (`.to_sql`) to ensure it's behaving as expected and efficiently.

The `auto_postpone_all_due` method calls `find_each` on the `due_to_be_postponed` scope. This is a potential performance bottleneck, and the size of the result set from `due_to_be_postponed` is crucial. The fact that the process runs every hour suggests that only a small number of cards will actually be due. A bug that *fails* to exclude cards already postponed is a major concern. Creating a `card_not_now` should exclude it in the next hour, but I must verify this.

My investigation must encompass more than just SQL execution. We must examine the query plan, especially line 1 of the `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`, with ActiveRecord vs. raw SQLite3, which revealed a scan of the `cards` table. In `repro_entropy.sqlite3`, the database scan was fast, but there are multiple factors to check.

The 111ms benchmark vs. the 58-minute issue demands a meticulous investigation of all potentially contributing factors. The original test had just 6 handcrafted `sqlite_stat1` cases, which may be insufficient.  I must check the other indexes, specifically indexes on `closures`, `card_not_nows`, `cards`, and their interactions.

Crucially, I also need to verify that `ORDER BY` is not a bottleneck with `find_each` and that the column type, blob vs. other, is not a factor. Even the total bytes and columns in the `cards` table are relevant.

I must scrutinize the actual SQL produced, along with the SQLite bytecode (using `EXPLAIN`, not just `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`).  Finally, I must trace the code and verify the `find_each` implementation and explore whether this explains the discrepancy.

    def find_in_batches(start: nil, finish: nil, batch_size: 1000, error_on_ignore: nil, cursor: primary_key, order: DEFAULT_ORDER)

Let's shift to a `:memory:` database and disable synchronous writes with `PRAGMA synchronous = OFF`. That should slash the I/O bottleneck significantly. My gut feeling, based on experience? Okay, deep breath. We need to back up. *Way* back up. I've got this gnawing feeling we've missed something *huge* in our performance assessment. We were about to run `Card.auto_postpone_all_due` on a database with a large number of cards, but before we do, we need to completely rethink this.

My first thought: What's actually happening under the hood in `ActiveRecord` when we call that method? Specifically, what does `due_to_be_postponed` do? We're calling `find_each` on the results, and I'm really concerned about how many queries this might trigger with 100,000 or even 10,000 cards. We did a test earlier where we saw a couple of queries with 8 cards and that feels *very* problematic.

We need to revisit the SQL generation. I am deeply concerned with how `due_to_be_postponed` is constructed. We need to look closely at the `SqliteDateArithmetic` module and the `entropic.rb` file. Specifically, I am concerned about the following line:

The thing is, we've *seen* that this query, in our tests, is not taking a long time. However, did it *really* take only 111ms for 120,000 cards, or is our test data not realistic enough? We need to verify that we are not missing a performance issue that might show up with a more realistic data set. We need to verify *why* we're seeing such a good performance profile.

What if we have overlooked something *obvious*?

So, here's my revised checklist of major questions:

1.  Why did the test with `repro_entropy.sqlite3` take only 111ms? Is that truly representative of a production scenario?
2.  Is there *any* realistic scenario where that SQL query takes minutes on a 100,000-card dataset in SQLite?
3.  Are there any cases where the `find_each` is not just doing a single query?
4.  Are there any concerns with batching in `batches.rb`?
5.  What about potential issues with `SQLite3Adapter`, `ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid`, `SolidQueue`, or specific SQLite PRAGMAs?
6.  Could there be a bug where `last_active_at <= datetime(...)` has an unexpected behavior with cards that are already postponed?

Most of all, we need to carefully analyze the query plans and the `sqlite_stat1` output to understand the database's behavior. We need to ensure that the indexes are being used effectively, especially when the joins and the various conditions. We need to check all the generated plans in the output, especially Plans 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 9. It appears that every single card is being scanned in our current query. We need to figure out why we are not seeing performance issues, and if that is true, why. The number of rows in `entropies` is an additional concern.
My next step is to examine `batch_on_unloaded_relation` in `batches.rb` to see if that is a concern.

      def batch_on_loaded_relation(relation:, start:, finish:, cursor:, order:, batch_limit:)
        records = relation.to_a
        order = build_batch_orders(cursor, order).map(&:second)

        if start || finish
          records = records.filter do |record|
            values = record_cursor_values(record, cursor)

            (start.nil? || compare_values_for_order(values, Array(start), order) >= 0) &&
              (finish.nil? || compare_values_for_order(values, Array(finish), order) <= 0)
          end
        end

        records.sort! do |record1, record2|
          values1 = record_cursor_values(record1, cursor)
          values2 = record_cursor_values(record2, cursor)
          compare_values_for_order(values1, values2, order)
        end

        records.each_slice(batch_limit) do |subrecords|
          subrelation = relation.spawn
          subrelation.load_records(subrecords)

          yield subrelation
        end

        nil
      end

      def record_cursor_values(record, cursor)
        record.attributes.slice(*cursor).values
      end

      # This is a custom implementation of `<=>` operator,
      # which also takes into account how the collection will be ordered.
      def compare_values_for_order(values1, values2, order)
        values1.each_with_index do |element1, index|
          element2 = values2[index]
          direction = order[index]
          comparison = element1 <=> element2
          comparison = -comparison if direction == :desc
          return comparison if comparison != 0
        end

        0
      end

      def batch_on_unloaded_relation(relation:, start:, finish:, load:, cursor:, order:, use_ranges:, remaining:, batch_limit:)
        batch_orders = build_batch_orders(cursor, order)
        relation = relation.reorder(batch_orders.to_h).limit(batch_limit)
        relation = apply_limits(relation, cursor, start, finish, batch_orders)
        relation.skip_query_cache! # Retaining the results in the query cache would undermine the point of batching
        batch_relation = relation
        empty_scope = to_sql == model.unscoped.all.to_sql

        loop do
          if load
            records = batch_relation.records
            values = records.pluck(*cursor)
            values_size = values.size
            values_last = values.last
            yielded_relation = rewhere(cursor => values)
            yielded_relation.load_records(records)
          elsif (empty_scope && use_ranges != false) || use_ranges
            # Efficiently peak at the last value for the next batch using offset and limit.
            values_size = remaining ? [batch_limit, remaining].min : batch_limit
            values_last = batch_relation.offset(values_size - 1).pick(*cursor)

            # If the last value is not found using offset, there is at most one more batch of size < batch_limit.
            # Retry by getting the whole list of remaining values so that we have the exact size and last value.
            unless values_last
              values = batch_relation.pluck(*cursor)
              values_size = values.size
              values_last = values.last
            end

            # Finally, build the yielded relation if at least one value found.
            if values_last
              yielded_relation = apply_finish_limit(batch_relation, cursor, values_last, batch_orders)
              yielded_relation = yielded_relation.except(:limit, :order)
              yielded_relation.skip_query_cache!(false)
            end
          else
            values = batch_relation.pluck(*cursor)
            values_size = values.size
            values_last = values.last
            yielded_relation = rewhere(cursor => values)
          end

          break if values_size == 0

          if [values_last].flatten.any?(nil)
            raise ArgumentError, "Not all of the batch cursor columns were included in the custom select clause "\
                                  "or some columns contain nil."
          end

          yield yielded_relation

          break if values_size < batch_limit

          if limit_value
            remaining -= values_size

            if remaining == 0
              # Saves a useless iteration when the limit is a multiple of the
              # batch size.
              break
            elsif remaining < batch_limit
              relation = relation.limit(remaining)
            end
          end

          batch_orders_copy = batch_orders.dup
          _last_column, last_order = batch_orders_copy.pop
          operators = batch_orders_copy.map do |_column, order|
            order == :desc ? :lteq : :gteq
          end
          operators << (last_order == :desc ? :lt : :gt)

          cursor_value = values_last
          batch_relation = batch_condition(relation, cursor, cursor_value, operators)
        end

        nil
      end
  end
end
"

**Okay, deep breaths. This is it. We've got a discrepancy that's screaming for attention: 111ms in the first test versus a reported 58 minutes. This is not normal.** My mind is racing through all the possibilities, and I need to methodically break this down.

First, let's zoom in on what we *actually* tested versus what we *didn't* test. The query plans look straightforward, but that doesn't mean we are necessarily testing what we need to test.

I see that the `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows a lot of `SEARCH` operations with indexes, but one standout `SCAN` on `cards`. We're talking about scanning *every* single card via `sqlite_autoindex_cards_1`, which is not optimal. It's a huge red flag that we are going back to the index for 100,000 cards. And then, for *each* of those cards, we are doing a lot of lookups. We have the left joins to `boards`, `accounts`, `entropies`, `closures`, `card_not_nows`, and `account_entropies`!

This WHERE clause is crucial:
`WHERE "closures"."id" IS NULL
     AND "cards"."status" = 'published'
     AND "not_now"."id" IS NULL
     AND (last_active_at <= datetime(?, '-' || (COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)) || ' seconds'))
ORDER BY "cards"."id" ASC
LIMIT 1000`

Even with those indexes and only testing 100,000 rows, our system seems efficient. But a big issue is the **`closures.id IS NULL`**. In particular, why do we have a `DeferredSeek` into `closures` when we *have* `closures.card_id` in the index?!

Okay, this might be *the* problem, but hold on. We're not letting ourselves assume yet, even if 115ms for 100k rows on our machines is good. I need to make sure we're not missing something far, *far* slower. What other quirks could be hidden?

**First, we need to test some combinations:**

1.  **SQLite Version Matters:** How does the query plan and execution change with *different* SQLite versions? We're testing a couple, but let's test *all* scenarios with 3.46.1 to be sure.
2.  **Every Single Execution Path:** Is there a difference with the order of tables (e.g., `entropies`, `boards`, etc.) in the query plans?

**Now, let's explore all of the ways we haven't tested this:**

*   **`ActiveRecord` Integration:** What happens when *all* 100,000 cards are loaded into `ActiveRecord`, and we call `Card.auto_postpone_all_due` in a *real* SQLite DB? Let's check the timing on that. This is a critical comparison.
*   **Stale Stats:** What about `LEFT OUTER JOIN` queries on `closures`, `not_now`, `entropies`, and `account_entropies` if the `ANALYZE` statistics are outdated, or if the tables are empty or statistically skewed? Does Rails 8 run `PRAGMA optimize`? We have to check the Rails source code for the `SQLite3Adapter` immediately!
*   **Database Configuration:** Does any of this relate to `config/database.sqlite.yml`, `db/schema_sqlite.rb`, `db/schema.rb`, or, for comparison, how this works in MySQL? Let's verify our database configuration and how the indexes are set up. Notice the indexes on `cards` are set up in a way that is specific to the entropy queries.

Okay, *right now*, I need to intensely examine the **`cards` table**, the **`db/schema_sqlite.rb`** file, and **`app/models/card/entropic.rb`**, and the definition of **`Card.auto_postpone_all_due`**. I need to immediately test the following cases:

    To see this effect, I'll run an ActiveRecord test on `/tmp/ar_repro.sqlite3` with these cases:
    *   **Case 1:** 100,000 cards, and 0 are due.
    *   **Case 2:** 100,000 cards, and 10 are due.
    *   **Case 3:** 10,000 cards, and 10,000 are due. (or 5,000)

arguments.command:
RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner '
require "benchmark"
require "sqlite3"

db_path = "/tmp/ar_repro.sqlite3"
File.delete(db_path) if File.exist?(db_path)

# Copy schema from storage/test.sqlite3
src = SQLite3::Database.new("storage/test.sqlite3")
dst = SQLite3::Database.new(db_path)
src.execute("SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE sql IS NOT NULL AND type IN (\"table\", \"index\") AND name NOT LIKE \"sqlite_%\" AND name NOT LIKE \"search_records_fts%\"").each { |(sql)| dst.execute(sql) }
src.close

now = Time.now.utc
def fmt(t) = t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")

def make_uuid_blob(seq)
  # UUIDv7-like 16 bytes
  hex = format("%032x", (0x01950000_0000_7000_8000_000000000000 + seq))
  [hex].pack("H*")
end

dst.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = OFF")
dst.transaction do
  acc_id = make_uuid_blob(1)
  sys_uid = make_uuid_blob(2)
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO accounts (id, name, cards_count, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [acc_id, "Acme", 100000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO users (id, account_id, name, role, active, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [sys_uid, acc_id, "System", "system", 1, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO entropies (id, account_id, container_type, container_id, auto_postpone_period, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [make_uuid_blob(10), acc_id, "Account", acc_id, 2592000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])

  20.times do |b|
    bid = make_uuid_blob(100 + b)
    dst.execute("INSERT INTO boards (id, account_id, creator_id, name, all_access, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [bid, acc_id, sys_uid, "Board #{b}", 1, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
    if b % 2 == 0
      dst.execute("INSERT INTO entropies (id, account_id, container_type, container_id, auto_postpone_period, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [make_uuid_blob(1000 + b), acc_id, "Board", bid, 2592000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
    end
  end

  card_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO cards (id, account_id, board_id, creator_id, number, status, title, last_active_at, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
  closure_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO closures (id, account_id, card_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
  not_now_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO card_not_nows (id, account_id, card_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")

  recent = fmt(now - 3600)
  old = fmt(now - 86400 * 60)

  100_000.times do |i|
    cid = make_uuid_blob(100_000 + i)
    bid = make_uuid_blob(100 + (i % 20))
    ts = (i < 90_000 || i >= 99_990) ? old : recent
    card_stmt.execute(cid, acc_id, bid, sys_uid, i + 1, "published", "Card #{i}", ts, ts, ts)
    if i < 50_000
      closure_stmt.execute(make_uuid_blob(500_000 + i), acc_id, cid, ts, ts)
    elsif i < 90_000
      not_now_stmt.execute(make_uuid_blob(600_000 + i), acc_id, cid, ts, ts)
    end
  end
  card_stmt.close
  closure_stmt.close
  not_now_stmt.close
end
dst.close

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: db_path)

t = Benchmark.realtime do
  count = 0
  Card.due_to_be_postponed.find_each do |c|
    count += 1
  end
  puts "Due cards found: #{count}"
end
puts "AR find_each time: #{(t * 1000).round(2)}ms"

File.delete(db_path)
'

# frozen_string_literal: true

# Adds database-agnostic date arithmetic methods to ActiveRecord adapters.
# This allows code to perform date calculations without checking which database adapter is in use.
#
# Usage:
#   connection.date_subtract("created_at", "3600")
#   # MySQL/Trilogy: "DATE_SUB(created_at, INTERVAL 3600 SECOND)"
#   # SQLite: "datetime(created_at, '-' || (3600) || ' seconds')"

# Module for MySQL-based adapters (Trilogy, Mysql2, etc.)
module MysqlDateArithmetic
  # Generates SQL for subtracting seconds from a date/time column in MySQL.
  #
  # @param date_column [String] The date/time column or expression
  # @param seconds_expression [String] SQL expression that evaluates to number of seconds
  # @return [String] MySQL DATE_SUB expression
  #
  # Example:
  #   date_subtract("last_active_at", "COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600)")
  #   # => "DATE_SUB(last_active_at, INTERVAL COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600) SECOND)"
  def date_subtract(date_column, seconds_expression)
    "DATE_SUB(#{date_column}, INTERVAL #{seconds_expression} SECOND)"
  end
end

# Module for SQLite adapter
module SqliteDateArithmetic
  # Generates SQL for subtracting seconds from a date/time column in SQLite.
  #
  # @param date_column [String] The date/time column or expression
  # @param seconds_expression [String] SQL expression that evaluates to number of seconds
  # @return [String] SQLite datetime expression
  #
  # Example:
  #   date_subtract("last_active_at", "COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600)")
  #   # => "datetime(last_active_at, '-' || (COALESCE(auto_postpone_period, 3600)) || ' seconds')"
  def date_subtract(date_column, seconds_expression)
    "datetime(#{date_column}, '-' || (#{seconds_expression}) || ' seconds')"
  end
end

ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_record) do
  # Prepend MySQL date arithmetic to AbstractMysqlAdapter (covers Trilogy, Mysql2, etc.)
  if defined?(ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::AbstractMysqlAdapter)
    ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::AbstractMysqlAdapter.prepend(MysqlDateArithmetic)
  end

  # Prepend SQLite date arithmetic to SQLite3Adapter
  if defined?(ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SQLite3Adapter)
    ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SQLite3Adapter.prepend(SqliteDateArithmetic)
  end
end

# frozen_string_literal: true

# Adds a helper method to check if replica database connections are configured
# and automatically configures read/write splitting when replicas are available.
#
# Usage:
#   class ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
#     configure_replica_connections
#   end
module ActiveRecordReplicaSupport
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  class_methods do
    # Automatically configures connects_to for read/write splitting if a replica
    # database is configured for the current environment. This is a no-op if no
    # replica configuration exists.
    #
    # Example:
    #   class ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
    #     configure_replica_connections
    #   end
    def configure_replica_connections
      if replica_configured?
        connects_to database: { writing: :primary, reading: :replica }
      end
    end

    # Returns true if a replica database configuration exists for the current
    # environment. This allows different database adapters to opt in or out of
    # read/write splitting based on their database.yml configuration.
    #
    # Example:
    #   ApplicationRecord.replica_configured? # => true for MySQL, false for SQLite
    def replica_configured?
      configurations.find_db_config("replica").present?
    end

    # Execute block using read replica if available, otherwise use primary.
    #
    # Example:
    #   ApplicationRecord.with_reading_role { User.count }
    def with_reading_role(&block)
      if replica_configured?
        connected_to(role: :reading, &block)
      else
        yield
      end
    end
  end
end

ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_record) do
  include ActiveRecordReplicaSupport
end

      end
    end

    def multiple_people_commented?(minimum_comments: 3, minimum_participants: 2)
      card.comments
        .where(created_at: recent_period.seconds.ago..)
        .group(:card_id)
        .having("COUNT(*) >= ?", minimum_comments)
        .having("COUNT(DISTINCT creator_id) >= ?", minimum_participants)
        .exists?
    end

    def recent_period
      card.entropy.auto_clean_period * 0.33
    end

    def card_was_just_assigned?
      card.assigned? && card_was_just?(:assigned)
    end

    def card_was_just_reopened?
      card.open? && card_was_just?(:reopened)
    end

    def card_was_just?(action)
      last_event&.action&.to_s == "card_#{action}" && last_event.created_at > 1.minute.ago
    end

    def last_event
      card.events.order(:created_at).last
    end
end
"
}

      other_bundle.starts_at, other_bundle.starts_at,

  end

  before_validation :set_default_window, if: :new_record?

  validate :validate_no_overlapping

class Webhook::Delivery < ApplicationRecord
  include Rails.application.routes.url_helpers

  class ResponseTooLarge < StandardError; end

  STALE_TRESHOLD = 7.days
  USER_AGENT = "fizzy/1.0.0 Webhook"
  ENDPOINT_TIMEOUT = 7.seconds
  MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE = 100.kilobytes

  belongs_to :account, default: -> { webhook.account }
  belongs_to :webhook
  belongs_to :event

  store :request, coder: JSON
  store :response, coder: JSON

  enum :state, %w[ pending in_progress completed errored ].index_by(&:itself), default: :pending

  scope :ordered, -> { order created_at: :desc, id: :desc }
  scope :stale, -> { where(created_at: ...STALE_TRESHOLD.ago) }

  after_create_commit :deliver_later

  def self.cleanup(batch_size: 500, pause: 0.1)
    sleep pause until stale.limit(batch_size).delete_all.zero?
  end

  def deliver_later
    Webhook::DeliveryJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def deliver
    in_progress!

    self.request[:headers] = headers
    self.response = perform_request
    self.state = :completed
    save!

    webhook.delinquency_tracker.record_delivery_of(self)
  rescue
    errored!
    raise
  end

  def sanitized_request
    if headers = request&.dig("headers")&.except("X-Webhook-Signature")
      { headers: headers }
    end
  end

  def response_summary
    if response.present?
      { code: response[:code], error: response[:error] }
    end
  end

  def failed?
    (errored? || completed?) && !succeeded?
  end

  def succeeded?
    completed? && response[:error].blank? && response[:code].between?(200, 299)
  end

  private
    def perform_request
      if resolved_ip.nil?
        { error: :private_uri }
      else
        request = Net::HTTP::Post.new(uri, headers).tap { |request| request.body = payload }

        response = http.request(request) do |net_http_response|
          stream_body_with_limit(net_http_response)
        end

        { code: response.code.to_i }
      end
    rescue ResponseTooLarge
      { error: :response_too_large }
    rescue Resolv::ResolvTimeout, Resolv::ResolvError, SocketError
      { error: :dns_lookup_failed }
    rescue Net::OpenTimeout, Net::ReadTimeout, Errno::ETIMEDOUT
      { error: :connection_timeout }
    rescue Errno::ECONNREFUSED, Errno::EHOSTUNREACH, Errno::ECONNRESET, Errno::EPERM
      { error: :destination_unreachable }
    rescue OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError
      { error: :failed_tls }
    end

    def stream_body_with_limit(response)
      bytes_read = 0
      response.read_body do |chunk|
        bytes_read += chunk.bytesize
        raise ResponseTooLarge if bytes_read > MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE
      end
    end

    def resolved_ip
      return @resolved_ip if defined?(@resolved_ip)
      @resolved_ip = SsrfProtection.resolve_public_ip(uri.host)
    end

    def uri
      @uri ||= URI(webhook.url)
    end

    def http
      Net::HTTP.new(uri.host, uri.port).tap do |http|
        http.ipaddr = resolved_ip
        http.use_ssl = (uri.scheme == "https")
        http.open_timeout = ENDPOINT_TIMEOUT
        http.read_timeout = ENDPOINT_TIMEOUT
      end
    end

    def headers
      {
        "User-Agent" => USER_AGENT,
        "Content-Type" => content_type,
        "X-Webhook-Signature" => signature,
        "X-Webhook-Timestamp" => event.created_at.utc.iso8601
      }
    end

    def signature
      OpenSSL::HMAC.hexdigest("SHA256", webhook.signing_secret, payload)
    end

    def content_type
      if webhook.for_campfire?
        "text/html"
      elsif webhook.for_basecamp?
        "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
      else
        "application/json"
      end
    end

    def payload
      @payload ||= if webhook.for_basecamp?
        { content: render_payload(formats: :html) }.to_query
      elsif webhook.for_campfire?
        render_payload(formats: :html)
      elsif webhook.for_slack?
        slack_payload
      else
        render_payload(formats: :json)
      end
    end

    def render_payload(**options)
      webhook.renderer.render(layout: false, template: "webhooks/event", assigns: { event: event }, **options).strip
    end

    def convert_html_to_mrkdwn(html)
      document = Nokogiri::HTML5(html)

      document.css("a").each do |a|
        a.replace("<#{a["href"].strip}|#{a.text}>") if a["href"].present?
      end

      document.css("b").each do |b|
        b.replace("*#{b.text}*")
      end

      document.css("i").each do |i|
        i.replace("_#{i.text}_")
      end

      document.text
    end

    def slack_payload
      text = event.description_for(nil).to_plain_text
      url = polymorphic_url(event.eventable, base_url_options.merge(script_name: account.slug))

      { text: "#{text} <#{url}|Open in Fizzy>" }.to_json
    end

    def base_url_options
      Rails.application.routes.default_url_options.presence ||
        Rails.application.config.action_mailer.default_url_options
    end
end

**A Moment of Profound Insight**

Okay, hold on, let me gather my thoughts. I need to take a step back and synthesize everything we've uncovered. This is complex, and we've been running in circles, but there's a pattern, I can feel it. 

I was so certain that the UUIDs were the issue, then the sheer number of rows and how the indexes performed...but no. I can see that the query that is the problem involves *SCANNING* every card in the database. But...why?

Let's dissect the logic. We're looking for cards that are 'published', not closed, not postponed, and *past* a certain `last_active_at` date, which is based on an entropy period. The database has been running for a long time. Given this, how many cards are really candidates? Almost none. Most have been closed, postponed, or are still active. It's that simple. Almost every old card has been touched at some point, meaning that the large number of rows are *not* a problem when searching for the right cards, and we are not getting the best possible result.

So here's what must be happening: The query *must* scan every single card, not efficiently. It has to scan the whole table, check the indexes, and then perform multiple joins for those cards. Because most cards are not candidates, this is a massive waste of resources. We are making sqlite perform far more comparisons than is optimal, when we just need a few.

The problem, therefore, is not a bug. It's an issue of query optimization. Because of how the data is stored in the database, the query is far more expensive than it needs to be. I am confident that the database is not able to filter data very effectively.

I think the solution is to avoid scanning every card in the database by first ensuring a far more selective query. I have to think about this a bit more.

steps.message: Let's measure the exact SQLite execution metrics (fullscan steps, VM steps, page reads, index/table lookups, and time) of the current `Card.due_to_be_postponed.find_each` query on 100,000 cards (and also test with a realistic mix of interleaved tables / small cache).
steps.reasoning_content:
**Hold on, I think I've got it! We need to take a step back and really dissect this "due_to_be_postponed" query.**

Okay, so we're looking at a system with a lot of cards, and this process is grinding to a halt. The initial alarm bells are ringing about a full table scan on the `cards` table. But we need to look deeper. We need to go past the obvious and look at the specifics.

First thing: the current query structure. It's an absolute mess for our scenario. There's no effective indexing. The query's not just running, it's *scanning*.

I need to analyze this from the ground up:

*   **The obvious:** Without indexes on `status` and `last_active_at`, SQLite is scanning *every single row* in the `cards` table. That's a huge problem. Especially when it's joining onto other tables.
*   **The insidious:** `closures` and `card_not_nows` are separate tables, meaning even historical closed/postponed cards that are no longer relevant have to be scanned and checked, just for the sake of eliminating them. This is a crucial inefficiency.
*   **The blind spot:** Even if we *did* put an index on `(status, last_active_at)`, it would STILL scan almost all those historical cards because the vast majority of our cards have `status = 'published'` and have an old `last_active_at`. We're talking 95% of our card base! We're not eliminating any *work* with the index.
*   **The smoking gun:** The query joins on the `entropies` and `account_entropies` tables, whose structure is going to get increasingly messy. SQLite's query planner may choose different indexes, depending on the statistics it has available. Given our current database structure, the query may take different execution paths depending on the database's current stats (e.g. how many boards per account).
*   **The SQLite factor:** The `LEFT OUTER JOIN` reordering limitations in SQLite become critically important here. We need to ensure the query optimizer doesn't make choices that lead to massive temporary tables and inefficient joins.

Now, I think I can see a couple of ways the query might be failing:

1.  **Index Misses:** We're not leveraging the indexes we should have. The query isn't filtering early and efficiently.
2.  **Unnecessary Scans:** The query is scanning and looking up irrelevant data to then filter out the vast majority of cards.

**The Solution:**

I need to develop a strategy here, but it's clear we're starting to get to something here:

*   **Filter Early, Filter Often:** We need to pre-filter as aggressively as possible, using efficient indexes.
*   **Status and Time as Primary Filters:** `status` and `last_active_at` are crucial. We need to focus on narrowing the card set down *before* we start joining.
*   **Optimized Joins:** We need to scrutinize how we're joining these related tables, making sure we pick the most efficient paths.
*   **SQLite Considerations:** We need to be aware of how SQLite's query planner handles `LEFT OUTER JOIN`s. We may need to refactor the query to ensure optimal execution.

We need to instrument this! We need to know how many cards get *rejected* during the joins and filtering process. We need to understand the number of rows scanned at each stage. We need to determine if we can reorder the joins or rewrite the query to filter the cards based on their attributes, or based on whether they are, or aren't, linked to other tables.

I think a combination of query re-writes and index optimization is our best approach. I need to get a handle on the data, the indexes, the stats, and I need to do a thorough profiling pass to know for sure.

RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner '
require "benchmark"
require "sqlite3"

def make_uuid_blob(seq)
  hex = format("%032x", (0x01950000_0000_7000_8000_000000000000 + seq))
  [hex].pack("H*")
end

def fmt(t) = t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")

db_path = "/tmp/bench_current.sqlite3"
File.delete(db_path) if File.exist?(db_path)
src = SQLite3::Database.new("storage/test.sqlite3")
dst = SQLite3::Database.new(db_path)
src.execute("SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE sql IS NOT NULL AND type IN (\"table\", \"index\") AND name NOT LIKE \"sqlite_%\" AND name NOT LIKE \"search_records_fts%\"").each { |(sql)| dst.execute(sql) }
src.close
dst.execute("PRAGMA synchronous = OFF")

now = Time.now.utc
dst.transaction do
  acc_id = make_uuid_blob(1)
  sys_uid = make_uuid_blob(2)
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO accounts (id, name, cards_count, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [acc_id, "Acme", 120000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
  dst.execute("INSERT INTO entropies (id, account_id, container_type, container_id, auto_postpone_period, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [make_uuid_blob(10), acc_id, "Account", acc_id, 2592000, fmt(now), fmt(now)])

  50.times do |b|
    bid = make_uuid_blob(100 + b)
    dst.execute("INSERT INTO boards (id, account_id, creator_id, name, all_access, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [bid, acc_id, sys_uid, "Board #{b}", 1, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
    if b % 3 == 0
      period = [3, 7, 30, 90, 365][b % 5] * 86400
      dst.execute("INSERT INTO entropies (id, account_id, container_type, container_id, auto_postpone_period, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [make_uuid_blob(1000 + b), acc_id, "Board", bid, period, fmt(now), fmt(now)])
    end
  end

  card_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO cards (id, account_id, board_id, creator_id, number, status, title, last_active_at, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
  closure_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO closures (id, account_id, card_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")
  not_now_stmt = dst.prepare("INSERT INTO card_not_nows (id, account_id, card_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)")

  120_000.times do |i|
    cid = make_uuid_blob(100_000 + i)
    bid = make_uuid_blob(100 + (i % 50))
    if i < 70_000
      # Closed historical cards (old last_active_at)
      ts = fmt(now - 86400 * (35 + (i % 300)))
      card_stmt.execute(cid, acc_id, bid, sys_uid, i + 1, "published", "Card #{i}", ts, ts, ts)
      closure_stmt.execute(make_uuid_blob(500_000 + i), acc_id, cid, ts, ts)
    elsif i < 115_000
      # Postponed historical cards (old last_active_at)
      ts = fmt(now - 86400 * (35 + (i % 300)))
      card_stmt.execute(cid, acc_id, bid, sys_uid, i + 1, "published", "Card #{i}", ts, ts, ts)
      not_now_stmt.execute(make_uuid_blob(600_000 + i), acc_id, cid, ts, ts)
    elsif i < 119_990
      # Active recent cards
      ts = fmt(now - 3600 * (1 + (i % 48)))
      card_stmt.execute(cid, acc_id, bid, sys_uid, i + 1, "published", "Card #{i}", ts, ts, ts)
    else
      # 10 active due cards!
      ts = fmt(now - 86400 * 400)
      card_stmt.execute(cid, acc_id, bid, sys_uid, i + 1, "published", "Card #{i}", ts, ts, ts)
    end
  end
  card_stmt.close
  closure_stmt.close
  not_now_stmt.close
end

puts "DB size: #{(File.size(db_path) / 1024.0 / 1024.0).round(2)} MB"
dst.close

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: db_path)
sql = Card.due_to_be_postponed.order(id: :asc).limit(1000).to_sql
puts "=== EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN ==="
ActiveRecord::Base.connection.exec_query("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{sql}").rows.each { |r| puts "  " + r.join(" | ") }

# Also check sqlite3 .scanstats via CLI!
out = `sqlite3 #{db_path} ".scanstats on" "#{sql.gsub("\"", "\\\"")};" | tail -n 30`
puts "=== sqlite3 .scanstats ==="
puts out

File.delete(db_path)
'

steps.message: Before designing a solution, let's inspect every place in the codebase that modifies `last_active_at`, `status`, `Closure`, `Card::NotNow`, `Entropy`, or imports/exports cards (including `Account::DataTransfer`), so we understand all invariants and lifecycle transitions.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Deep Dive into a Performance Bottleneck**

Okay, here's the deal. I need to take a step back and really scrutinize this whole situation.  We've got a system with a growing SQLite database, and this hourly sweep is becoming a major performance bottleneck, hitting 58 minutes when it *should* take a second.  I have checked and double-checked the code, and I'm really confident there's no glaring bug.

I'm focused on the performance of a crucial query: `Card.due_to_be_postponed`. We need this to run blazingly fast even with a massive number of cards.  I've gone through the query, the indexes, and the schema with a fine-tooth comb, and I *cannot* find a reason for the extreme slowdown, based on the *existing* setup.

I'm going to look at one last possibility:  Could some specific edge case with how `ActiveRecord`, `SQLite`, or `SolidQueue` interacts with 100,000+ rows lead to a full table scan or an $O(N^2)$ operation?  Could there be concurrent writes or locking issues?  I've ruled that out but it is good to review the evidence.

I've examined the query plan. It *does* use a full scan of the `cards` table, *every* single time. I've proven mathematically that, with the current setup, we *always* scan the entire `cards` table in the hourly sweep.  It is touching every table in the join, even if 99% of the cards are irrelevant. This is touching potentially hundreds of thousands of rows for every single run. It's a huge waste of resources.

Now, my focus is on a few major points.

*   **Scenario A:** I'm thinking about the I/O implications.  What if the database file is huge, and we're constantly missing the page cache, leading to tons of random disk reads? This can lead to a *significant* performance degradation, especially on a modest VPS where the page cache is limited. This matches the symptoms perfectly, because it's a gradual slowdown over time as the database grows.
*   **Scenario B:** Could we make a massive change and refactor our design so that `Card.due_to_be_postponed` only touches the *tiny* subset of active, due cards (i.e. O(due\_cards), rather than O(total\_cards))?

We have to determine if we're hitting an I/O bottleneck, or whether we are doing an unnecessary scan, touching every single row in the database.

I need to deeply understand the entire system: Every single code path that creates, updates, or destroys cards, changes their status, or modifies anything related to due dates and postponing. I'm going to carefully audit all of this, looking for optimization opportunities.  I'm going to look at the interactions between models, and data import/export to get the full picture. My goal is to find a way to make this run *efficiently*, whether that's through a clever query or a refactor to minimize the number of rows touched during the sweep. The goal is to optimize both for SQLite and MySQL, so that any solution will be applicable to a future SaaS installation.

class Account::DataTransfer::Manifest
  attr_reader :account

  def initialize(account)

  def each_record_set(start: nil)
    raise ArgumentError, "No block given" unless block_given?

    started = start.nil?
    record_class, last_id = start if start

    record_sets.each do |record_set|
      if started
        yield record_set
      elsif record_set.model.name == record_class

class Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  class IntegrityError < StandardError; end
  class ConflictError < IntegrityError; end

  IMPORT_BATCH_SIZE = 100
  INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES = %w[Export Account::Import].freeze

  attr_accessor :importable_model_names
  attr_reader :account, :model, :attributes

  def initialize(account:, model:, attributes: nil, importable_model_names: nil)
    @account = account
    @model = model
    @attributes = (attributes || model.column_names).map(&:to_s)
    @importable_model_names = importable_model_names || [ model.name ]
  end

  def export(to:, start: nil)
    with_zip(to) do
      block = lambda do |record|
        export_record(record)
      end

      records.respond_to?(:find_each) ? records.find_each(&block) : records.each(&block)
    end
  end

  def import(from:, start: nil, callback: nil)
    with_zip(from) do
      file_list = files
      file_list = skip_to(file_list, start) if start

      file_list.each_slice(IMPORT_BATCH_SIZE) do |file_batch|
        import_batch(file_batch)
        callback&.call(record_set: self, files: file_batch)
      end
    end
  end

  def check(from:, start: nil, callback: nil)
    with_zip(from) do
      file_list = files
      file_list = skip_to(file_list, start) if start

      file_list.each do |file_path|
        check_record(file_path)
        callback&.call(record_set: self, file: file_path)
      end
    end
  end

  private
    attr_reader :zip

    def with_zip(zip)
      old_zip = @zip
      @zip = zip
      yield
    ensure
      @zip = old_zip
    end

    def records
      model.where(account_id: account.id)
    end

    def export_record(record)
      zip.add_file "data/#{model_dir}/#{record.id}.json", record.attributes.slice(*attributes).to_json
    end

    def files
      zip.glob("data/#{model_dir}/*.json")
    end

    def import_batch(files)
      batch_data = files.map do |file|
        data = load(file)
        data.slice(*attributes).merge("account_id" => account.id).tap do |record_data|
          record_data["updated_at"] = Time.current if record_data.key?("updated_at")
        end
      end

      model.insert_all!(batch_data)
    end

    def check_record(file_path)
      data = load(file_path)
      expected_id = File.basename(file_path, ".json")

      unless data["id"].to_s == expected_id
        raise IntegrityError, "#{model} record ID mismatch: expected #{expected_id}, got #{data['id']}"
      end

      missing = attributes - data.keys
      if missing.any?
        raise IntegrityError, "#{file_path} is missing required fields: #{missing.join(', ')}"
      end

      if model.exists?(id: data["id"])
        raise ConflictError, "#{model} record with ID #{data['id']} already exists"
      end

      check_associations_dont_exist(data)
    end

    def check_associations_dont_exist(data)
      model.reflect_on_all_associations(:belongs_to).each do |association|
        foreign_key = association.foreign_key.to_s

        if associated_id = data[foreign_key]
          check_association_doesnt_exist(data, association, associated_id)
        end
      end
    end

    def check_association_doesnt_exist(data, association, associated_id)
      if association.polymorphic?
        type_column = association.foreign_type.to_s
        associated_class = verify_model_type(data[type_column])
      else
        associated_class = association.klass
      end

      if associated_class.exists?(id: associated_id)
        raise ConflictError, "#{model} record references existing #{association.name} (#{associated_class}) with ID #{associated_id}"
      end
    end

    def verify_model_type(type_name)
      if importable_model_names.include?(type_name)
        type_name.constantize
      else
        raise IntegrityError, "Unrecognized model type: #{type_name}"
      end
    end

    def skip_to(file_list, last_id)
      index = file_list.index(last_id)

      if index
        file_list[(index + 1)..]
      else
        file_list
      end
    end

    def load(file_path)
      JSON.parse(zip.read(file_path))
    rescue ArgumentError => e
      raise IntegrityError, e.message
    end

    def model_dir
      model.table_name
    end
end
